sentences: Sunlight slants into an almost empty room and leaves bright patches on the floorboards.
The only person here is a woman with her back to us.
This is Interior in Strandgade, Sunlight on the Floor, painted in 1901 by the Danish artist Vilhelm Hammershøi.
Hammershøi was born in Copenhagen in 1864 and died there in 1916.
For a little over ten years from 1898 he lived at Strandgade 30, an old building in the Christianshavn district of the city, and he painted the rooms of that flat again and again.
The woman is usually taken to be his wife, Ida, who appears in many of these interiors.
She never shows us her face.
We cannot tell what she is doing, or what she might be thinking, and the painter does not want us to know.
Now look at the sunlight on the floor.
The square patches of light carry the pattern of the window frames.
The light from the window draws a second window across the floor.
Look at the colours.
Grey, white and pale brown are almost all there is.
Hammershøi deliberately held colour back, and the room falls into a deep silence.
That is why he is so often called a painter of silence.
The lines of the door, the walls and the floorboards are straight and orderly, and there is hardly any furniture.
The room seems to exist not for decoration or for daily life, but for light and space themselves.
In Hammershøi's pictures, doors often lead on into further rooms, half seen or not seen at all.
Following them, you feel as if you were walking slowly through the flat yourself.
Taken together, his paintings of Strandgade 30 build up one quiet, connected home, room by room, in changing light.
This quiet interior recalls the Dutch painters of the seventeenth century, such as Vermeer, who also watched the light from a window fall across a room.
The difference is that Hammershøi has removed almost every trace of a story.
In his lifetime Hammershøi was admired across Europe, but after his death he was largely forgotten for decades.
Since the late twentieth century he has been rediscovered, and his quiet rooms now draw large crowds.
This interior belongs to SMK, the National Gallery of Denmark, in Copenhagen, not far from the street where it was painted.
Step back and stay with it for a moment.
In a room where nothing happens, only the sunlight slowly moves.
Today, try looking for a while at the light that falls across your own floor.
